messages.subject_clean: [BioGeoBEARS] realized tip states in stochastic maps
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Apologies that it took me so long to figure this one out. Jonathan Drury was a great help by pointing out the bug and providing a workable example.

The issue here was due a previous "fix". In some cases, especially models that fit more poorly, or data that are very improbable under the model, the Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping script would have difficulty successfully simulating an event history along a branch.  One case might be sister species that are (EAIFDC, EAIFDC), but under DEC, the ancestral node would have a history of something like EAIFDC->E, EAIFDC, and then the "E" would have to evolve all the way to EAIFDC with just the right series of range addition events.  If the branch was short or "d" is low, this could be very improbable, such that the default "maxtries" (40,000) was not enough tries on that branch. This would produce a failed stochastic map, and if all of the stochastic maps fail then you don't get anything.

One solution was to increase maxtries, but cases were reported where even maxtries=1,000,000 weren't enough.  If you think about it, it is perfectly possible to have data configurations that have a probability of less than 1/1,000,000, especially under a poorly-fitting model, and especially when there are lots of areas and so the state space is huge.

So, the "fix" that was put in would, if maxtries is reached, proceed to "manually" figure out what series of range additions and range deletions was required to get from the stochastically mapped start state for the branch to the stochastically mapped end state (determination of these states is simulated first, dependent on the model etc.).  Then, it would put these in random order, subject to the constraint that no intermediate state is a null range.

The argument for this approach is, I think, convincing, which is that if the relevant history is so wildly improbable that the simulator can't find it after many tries, this means the necessary events are very rare, which means that probably only the minimum number of events occurred in that history, meaning it is OK (OK = a decent approximation of the process) to just list the events and place them in random order.

What Jonathan discovered was a bug in the fix.  Looking into it, I found out that at one point a "+1" in the (0-based) area index was not happening, meaning the wrong area was being assigned, and also the final state was not being added to the history.

I also discovered that, in small/fast datasets where stochastic mapping is rapid, for time-stratified analyses, the random seed (set by the computer clock) would not be changing fast enough, so some stochastic maps would be repeats of each other.  I've changed this so the seed is incremented in each for-loop so this doesn't happen. (This fix was made for the non-stratified analyses long ago, but I guess I never did it for the stratified analyses.)

These files have thus been revised, and are on PhyloWiki:

stochastic_map_given_inputs.R
BioGeoBEARS_stochastic_mapping_v1.R
runBSM_v1.R

They can be sourced like usual.  Probably this wasn't that common of an issue, and these problematic branches are typically rare anyway. But it's best to announce it for the record.

Cheers!  And keep bug reports coming, even if I don't get to them right away.

Nick

messages.body_plain:
Here is an email I just sent on the basics of Biogeographic Stochastic Mapping (BSM), and interpreting plots.

I am anonymizing it to post more generally, as it may help others. I've also added more headers and links.

Cheers!
Nick

> On Sun, May 8, 2016 at 3:51 PM, XXX wrote:
> Dear Nick,
>
> I'm struggling to understand the BSM outputs, but I have found little (or none) advance so far.
>
> I was able to run the analysis with your wonderfully clear scripts, but I still have no idea how to interpret the histograms (I have attached here one example).
>
> Today I came across this nice paper on New World bats:
>
> http://sysbio.oxfordjournals.org/content/65/3/432.abstract
>
> and that helped me to better formulate my questions:
>
> 1) What exactly does "the most frequent modes of range inheritance" mean? How can I interpret that from the histogram? For example, in the bats paper the authors say "Range copying and range subset within the same large area represent 84.1% of the total number of events at cladogenesis, or 160 of the 191 nodes in the phylogeny".
>
> 2) Which also brings my next question: How can I correlate the histogram with each node of my phylogeny? How on Earth do they know that "Anagenetic dispersal was more frequent between the two continental regions, particularly from South America to Central and North America"? I would love to get that information for my dataset.
>
> I think the bottomline of my problem is to really understand what does the histogram mean, how to interpret it, and how I can correlate that information with my tree.
>
> I think that understanding this is the 'last frontier' to come with a full circle with my PhD investigation. Even if this analysis is just a complement to the main BGB results, I am sure that understanding it would enrich my discussion, and definitely help me to continue to scratch the surface of this amazing model-based biogeography.
>
> Thank you so much for all your attention so far! Have a nice weekend!
>
> XXX

Hi XXX!

Glad you're looking at BSM stuff!  Apologies that the documentation isn't all there, I haven't even had time to get the basic paper on the BSM method out yet! Thanks for the link to the SysBio paper ( http://sysbio.oxfordjournals.org/content/65/3/432.abstract ), I'm glad this stuff is getting used so fast, although it should be considered "beta" I guess until it is officially published.

DEFINITION OF "A HISTORY" (on a phylogeny)

As you know, in real-life biogeographic history, there was only one series of events (dispersal events etc.) that took place as a particular clade evolved.  The problem is that we don't know that exact history.  So, we are trying to *infer* that history, using various phylogenetic inference methods.

The True History, if we had it, would have an exact count of the number of events of each type that had occurred on the phylogeny, and each event would have taken place at an exact time.  Similarly, if we had the exact history of a DNA base, or of a morphological character, every substitution event would have occurred at some exact time point.

INFERRING ANCESTRAL STATE PROBABILITIES WITH MAXIMUM LIKELIHOOD / BAYESIAN INFERENCE

Of course, we don't have this history, so we have to infer it. The most common methods are likelihood and Bayesian, which both rely on stochastic models (transition rate matrices).  These methods are actually calculating the probability of the observed data *under all histories possible under the model*, conditional on the data and the inferred model parameters.  This is impressive, because there are an infinite number of exact histories.  These are the methods that, at each node, give you the probability of that node being in state 1, state 2, etc.  You can actually calculate these probabilities anywhere on the tree, not just at nodes, but nodes are computationally convenient.

TYPICAL MISTAKES MADE WHEN INTERPRETING ANCESTRAL STATE PROBABILITY PLOTS (or ancestral geographic range probability plots)

The main problem with these methods is that people often want to know more than just the probabilities -- they want to know when events occurred, and how many.  You can get a sense of this from looking at the probabilities plots, but it can be vague, and humans tend to over-simplify and interpret the probabilities plots in a "parsimony-thinking" sort of way.

Trying to count events "by eye" from the probability plot tends to produce:

(a) too few events,

(b) the timing is very vague ("probably between these two nodes"),

(c) over-interprets the probabilities (logic like this: "The most-probable range at node 10 is ABC, so I'll just assume it was ABC, even though ABC only had 10% of the total probability").

Problem (d) is that people want to directly convert ML-inferred parameters like d, e, and j into relative probabilities of events, but this cannot be done for several overlapping reasons
- j is a weight not a rate,
- DEC and other biogeography models have additional events at cladogenesis in addition to d and e events, and these interact in a complicated way; and
- everything interacts with the distribution of the ranges at the tips, especially if the models don't perfectly fit the data, and models never perfectly fit the data

WHAT BIOGEOGRAPHIC STOCHASTIC MAPPING IS DOING

All that stochastic mapping does is produce a series of exact histories that are all approximately equally probable "realizations" of the true history.  Each of these histories -- each "stochastic map" -- is a sample from the distribution of possible histories (conditional on the tree, model, model parameters, and data). Each exact history contains the exact events, their exact direction, and the exact time of each event.  Stochastic mapping is basically a form of conditional simulation.

By generating 50 or 100 of these histories (or 1000, as in that SysBio paper, although that's more than are really needed, 100 ought to be plenty, but for smaller datasets 1000 could still be fast), you can then get statistical distributions on (1) the number of events of each type, (2) their timing, (3) their direction, etc.

Physically counting the events, and looking for specific things (like a specific dispersal between area A and area B between 10 and 20 million years ago) can totally be done, by simple operations on R tables (data.frames).  But this requires some basic R skills with lists and tables, in order to manipulate the BSM output tables. (Try here: http://phylo.wikidot.com/2014-summer-research-experiences-sre-at-nimbios-for-undergra )

Basically, each stochastic map produces a table listing the cladogenetic events (=events at nodes), and their times and types etc., and a table listing the anagenetic events (= on branches).  These tables contain the time of the event, the type of event, etc.  Once you've learned out to count things in tables, etc., it's easy. (Also, you will have to understand the table column headings, but I think that should be fairly self-explanatory -- dangerous assumption I guess.)

FIGURING OUT NODE NUMBERS ON PHYLOGENETIC TREES, USING prt()

To find possible events near a particular node, you will have to find the APE node number for that node.  There are various methods, I like the BioGeoBEARS function prt(), which stands for "print tree to table".

This code is one way to do that:

trfn = "tree.newick"
tr = read.tree(trfn)
tr_table = prt(tr, get_tipnames=TRUE)

The table "tr_table" now has a row for each node or tip, the node number of that node, the length of the branch/edge below it, the list of tip names that descends from that node, etc.  I find this much easier to read than the default R tree format.

You will note that the events tables produced by BSM have a similar format to the prt() output tables.

Cheers, Nick

INTERPRETING HISTOGRAMS

P.S.: Interpreting the histograms: in that figure you send, all that was done was:

1. Look a one stochastic map (one possible exact history).

2. Count how many of each type of event there were in that one history.  E.g., 5 jump dispersal events, 30 sympatry/range copying events, 3 vicariance events, etc.

3. Repeat 1 and 2 50 times

4. Summarize those counts as histograms.  The histograms say these are the average number of events in one history:

anagenetic dispersal (d): 0
narrow sympatry (y): ~ 30
subset sympatry (s): ~10
vicariance (v): ~5
founder events (j): ~6

We could easily get standard deviations and 95% credibility intervals if we wanted.

Note that, in DEC or DEC+J, the weights of y, s, and v are the SAME. So you might naively expect the same number of each type of event. But this does not occur, because (a) weights convert to rates depending on the number of each type of event that is possible, and (b) the data will favor certain events over others.

Parameters and events under various models:
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#BioGeoBEARS_supermodel_graphic

Interpreting the weight parameters y, s, v, and j:
http://phylo.wikidot.com/per-event-weights-of-cladogenetic-range-inheritance-events-i

Cheers!
Nick

messages.body_plain:
On Mon, May 9, 2016 at 2:11 PM, x wrote:
> Hi Nick
>
> First dumb question: if I want to input an environmental distance file, is this a "BioGeoBEARS_run_object$dispersal_multipliers_fn" or "BioGeoBEARS_run_object$distsfn"? And should it be distances between regions or similarities?
>
> Also, I can't figure out whats wrong with my env distance file (attached), but I get this:
>
> > BioGeoBEARS_run_object$dispersal_multipliers_fn = "nmatrix_climaticdistance.txt"
>
> > BioGeoBEARS_run_object = readfiles_BioGeoBEARS_run(BioGeoBEARS_run_object)
>
> Warning message:
> In readLines(dispersal_multipliers_fn) :
>   incomplete final line found on 'nmatrix_climaticdistance.txt'
>
> Any ideas?
>
> thanks!
>
> XXX
>

Hi!

Quick points:

* Probably, put a blank line before the "END"
* The distance matrices, and the +x, +n models, are set up so that larger distances = lower dispersal probability, if x or n is negative.  But it would all work fine if you did 1/distance in the matrix, and then looked at values of x and n > 0.
* The manual dispersal multiplier matrix is a little different, typically people scale that between 0 and 1 as a literal hard-coded multiplier on dispersal probability.  But, again, it would work fine in other ways depending on what you do with w.

Re: environmental distances, to be totally standard you would add these lines for environmental distances (they are not in the basic intro script):

# Add environmental distances file
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$envdistsfn = "nmatrix_climaticdistance.txt"

# Add n as a free parameter (dispersal probs will be multiplied by env.distance^n)
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["n","type"] = "free"
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["n","init"] = 0
BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["n","est"] = 0

In general, these three things are slightly separate:

1. Manual dispersal multipliers ($dispersal_multipliers_fn)

Basic dispersal probabilities are multiplied by (dispersal_multiplier)^w

Default w = 1 (meaning, a literal interpretation of the manual dispersal multipliers)

This is a way to say, e.g. "I think dispersal between North America and Africa is 0.01 times as probable as dispersal between North America and South America".  The "w" parameter allows you to subject this sort of hypothesis to model testing, and or have the ML inference estimate the optimum scaling of your manual dispersal multiplier matrix. Not perfect but better than nothing.

2. Geographic distances ($distsfn)

Basic dispersal probabilities are multiplied by (geographic distance)^x

Default x = 0 (meaning, geographic distances play no role). If x is negative, dispersal probability declines with distance.

All distances must be >0. I recommend scaling distances so the minimum distance is 1, this means that e.g. d, j, etc. represent the rates for that minimum distance.

The +x model is a way to test if dispersal probabilities are influenced by some distance measure (centroid-to-centroid distance, closest-path-distance, travel time, whatever).  Each distance measure would constitute another hypothesis and another model to compare in a statistical model comparison.

The idea that dispersal probability should be modified by distance to the power x is also a hypothesis or model, which at some point should be compared to other functions of distance.  Whether or not it will be easy to distinguish different functions of distance, given typical datasets, which usually have less than 10 areas and thus around (10x10)/2 distances, is debatable.  In particular, we should expect that the tails of distributions may be difficult to distinguish.  But, it should be tried at some point (this would require some new BioGeoBEARS programming).

3. Environmental distances ($envdistsfn)

Basic dispersal probabilities are multiplied by (environmental distance)^x

Default x = 0 (meaning, environmental distances play no role). If x is negative, dispersal probability declines with environmental distance.

All distances must be >0. I recommend scaling distances so the minimum distance is 1, this means that e.g. d, j, etc. represent the rates for that minimum distance.

The +n model is a way to test if dispersal probabilities are influenced by some additional distance measure (centroid-to-centroid distance, closest-path-distance, travel time, whatever).  Each distance measure would constitute another hypothesis and another model to compare in a statistical model comparison.

Same comments for +n and +x models and their interpretation.

I added environmental distance as an obvious alternative/addition to the +x models.  But, these can all be combined.  And, if you wanted, you could throw geographic distance in envdistsfn, and environmental distance in distsfn, and it would work fine, the program "doesn't know the difference."  Also, if someone wanted, they could throw in even more distance matrices (this would take a little new programming).  I haven't done this yet, because soon the real question becomes, as with linear regression or any other correlational analysis, (a) what's your goal, (b) can you do a study more scientifically/intelligently than just throwing every imaginable predictor into an analysis and hoping the information you get from this data-dredging outweighs the statistical downsides of multiple testing, and the increasing difficulty of ML optimization searches with more and more parameters.

PS: I'll post an anonymous version of this to the BioGeoBEARS listserv as it may help others.

Cheers!
Nick

On Mon, May 9, 2016 at 9:13 AM, XXX wrote:
> Dear Nick,
>
> Thank you so much for the fast and great response! And please, don't apologise because you are by far the most attentive software developer I have contacted so far. I'm sure that this method will continue to be used, especially when it's officially published.
>
> I think I got the essence and theory behind the BSM, and it does make a ton of sense. This is why I want to include this in my work. But I still have a few lose ends in the practical area and the big picture of these results:
>
> 1) I do have some basic R skills and would love to try accessing these outputs in more detail. Could you give me a hint on how can I have access to each one of those tables generated by BGB for the BSM? I think I can found my way out on counting the events and the direction of those with what I've learned about R so far...I would love to try at the very least! As with the column headings, I'll take a look after getting access to the tables, and if I have any hint of doubt on their meaning I'll contact you just to make sure I got them right.
>
> 2) I'm still failing to relate those average number of events with the big picture for the evolution of the group I am studying. First, I know I can get the exact average values through R, right? But even with the interpretation 'by eye' of my histogram, am I right to say that 'narrow sympatry played a major role in the evolution of this group'? Because if yes, that makes a lot of sense because almost all these lineages are sympatric today. However, most importantly, I am also interested to see where in my tree those ~6 founder events and ~5 vicariant events  were most likely to have occurred. Does this even make sense, or am I interpreting this all wrong?
>
> I am really grateful for your superb support for BGB. Have a nice Sunday!
>
>
> Cheers,

> XXX

It sounds like you haven't actually looked at the PDFs that are produced?  If you run the full script here:
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeographical-stochastic-mapping-example-script

...one of the outputs is a PDF with, say, 50 copies of the phylogeny, each of them with a different mapping of the geographic history onto the phylogeny.  Looking at these, it should be obvious where the changes are occurring on your tree.

It's possible that your operating system doesn't automatically pop up the PDFs like mine does (I have a Mac).  To find the PDFs, go look in your working directory.

Anyway, once you have the PDFs to look at: these PDF graphics are just a graphical display of the information in the tables.

If you go through that example BSM script (you must go through scripts carefully and try to understand what is going on, not just copy-paste and treat it like a black box, I made the scripts to help people understand what they are doing by showing the basic steps!), you will see where RES_ana_events_tables and RES_clado_events_tables appear.  You would access them like this:

whatever$RES_ana_events_tables[[3]] --> this would get you the anagenetic events table for the third stochastic map stored in object "whatever".

whatever$RES_clado_events_tables[[3]] --> this would get you the cladogenetic events table for the same stochastic map.

* The function head() shows you just the first few lines of the table, which makes it easier to read.
* The function dim() shows you the number of rows and columns in the table
* The function names() shows you the column headings. You can then extract particular columns with e.g.:

whatever$RES_clado_events_tables[[3]]$nodes --> gets you the column with node numbers

> 2) I'm still failing to relate those average number of events with the big picture for the evolution of the group I am studying. First, I know I
> can get the exact average values through R, right? But even with the interpretation 'by eye' of my histogram, am I right to say that
> 'narrow sympatry played a major role in the evolution of this group'?

Yes, you are right to say 'narrow sympatry played a major role in the evolution of this group', and yes, this is because the number of such events is high, as measured by the histograms.

But: my comments about the problems with "interpreting by eye" were not about the histograms, they were about the ancestral-range-probabilities plots produced by default, non-stochastic-mapping BioGeoBEARS analyses

Example default ancestral-range-probabilities-plots:
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeographical-stochastic-mapping-example-script#pie_probs

Problems with "by-eye" interpretation of these plots for event counts:
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#Most_prob_states_not_joint

A single stochastic map:
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeographical-stochastic-mapping-example-script#single_BSM

A collection of stochastic maps:
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeographical-stochastic-mapping-example-script#animation_BSMs

The histograms are the actual estimates of the number of events of each type (conditional on the tree, model, ML parameters, and data. And the no-lineage-extinction assumption of all of these DEC-type methods).  They are not flawed "by-eye" estimates.

I think probably what you are really trying to get at is something about where the events occurred on your tree.  You can see this in the stochastic mapping PDF, but if you want to get more than that, you will have to parse the tables and figure out the node and branch numbers you are interested in. I gave you the basic scripts for doing this with prt(), but another way is by plotting the node numbers.

E.g.:

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've written a mini-FAQ on the issue that is sometimes observed with crashes / NaNs produced due to machine precision / underflow issues.  This assembles the bits of advice I've written many times, so that it is all in one place.  I will copy-paste it below (without formatting) to improve it's google-ability.  Please refer colleagues or posters to this, if you come across this issue.

Crashes / NaNs produced due to machine precision / underflow issues
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-errors-to-not-ignore#precision_crashes

Cheers!
Nick

Crashes / NaNs produced due to machine precision / underflow issues
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-errors-to-not-ignore#precision_crashes
=========================
Crashes / NaNs produced due to machine precision / underflow issues

(link to this section)

NOTE: All of this section constitutes my informed guess at what is going on when this error occurs. I am not an official computer scientist, nor an expert on the insides of R or how these might vary on all of the different computer systems people run R on. So: I Might Be Wrong, and Comments From People Who Know More are welcome.

The problem: Errors like this are sometimes observed:

rexpokit::expokit_dgpadm_Qmat(Qmat = Qmat, t =
     times, transpose_needed) : NA/NaN/Inf in foreign
     function call (arg 4)
Here is another one:

Error in eigen(nhatend) : infinite or missing values in 'x'
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In log(computed_likelihoods_at_each_node) : NaNs produced
2: In log(computed_likelihoods_at_each_node) : NaNs produced
3: In log(computed_likelihoods_at_each_node) : NaNs produced
4: In log(computed_likelihoods_at_each_node) : NaNs produced
Error in -details[[i, "hev"]] : invalid argument to unary operator
In addition: Warning message:
In optimx.run(par, optcfg$ufn, optcfg$ugr, optcfg$uhess, lower,  :
  Eigenvalue failure after method bobyqa
These sorts of errors seem to usually be due to machine precision issues, also called underflow errors.

Background on machine precision / underflow issues

(link to this section)

Background on "machine precision": Numbers in computers are, fundamentally, represented in binary — a series of bits, where each bit can take the value 0 or 1. This means that numbers with more precision require more bits — more space on the computer. Numbers with more precision will take more space. If you take a computer science class, this is one of the things you will be taught, but it may well be new to many biologists.

Because of machine precision, computers have different types of numbers: integers, long integers, floating point, "double" (double-precision floating-point), etc. Numbers with more precision require more bytes to store, and will take more computing time for the computer to process. For more information on this, see e.g. Wikipedia on single-precision floating point.

In "hard core" computing languages like C++, the programmer will decide ahead of time when different types of numbers will be used ("casting" or "typing" the numbers), and will also specify when conversions have to be made. This makes the code run faster, but makes programming much slower and more technical.

In more user-friendly languages like R, all of this "casting" or "typing" happens in the background. This is great because the programmer does not have to worry about it (usually), and it makes programming much easier, but this is one of the reasons that R programs run more slowly than equivalent programs in C++.

Background on "underflow": Because of limited precision on computers, numbers can only be so big or so small under a particular representation. In general, R is very good at managing these issues, but you can push it to the limit quite easily, if you know where to look.

For example, on my computer's version of R (64-bit Mac Pro), typing 1e-323 (or 1*10^-323) yields 9.881313e-324. Disturbingly, this is not exactly the same as the input 1e-323, and indicates we are near the minimum precision limit. If instead we type 1e-324, we get 0 returned. This is even worse, for example because dividing by 0 is undefined; in R, dividing something by 0 produces Inf (infinity). Again disturbingly, we know that 1e-323 is ten times bigger than 1e-324. So we know what the answer to 1e-323/1e-324 should be: it should just be 10. But if you type 1e-323/1e-324 into my computer, it thinks of it as 9.881313e-324/0, and produces the result Inf. This result is not just wrong, it's infinitely wrong!

(You should try this yourself on your own computer, and see where the default precision limit is; it might be different from my computer!)

This is an example of what is sometimes called an underflow error. Even worse ones are imaginable, for example where some calculation should produce a very small number, but instead produces a negative number. If the numbers are supposed to be probabilities, this result is Very Bad, because probabilities cannot be negative. For more, see Wikipedia on arithmetic underflow.

How the problem arises in BioGeoBEARS

(link to this section)

BioGeoBEARS, in order to speed up the slowest parts of the likelihood calculations, uses C++ (via the cladoRcpp package) and C++ and FORTRAN (via the rexpokit package) to perform some calculations more quickly. The "NaNs produced" error, when it occurs, seems to originate somewhere at this interface between R, C++, and FORTRAN. Furthermore, when it occurs, it seems to be machine-specific: R is cross-platform, and so are C++ and FORTRAN, but the latter two may be differently compiled on different operating systems, and the compilers may make different decisions about exactly how precision is treated. Usually, I cannot replicate someone's reported problem on my own computer (this may be because I have a very new, 64-bit Mac).

The problem seems to be more common in these situations:

- Windows machines
- Older machines
- "Bad" models (models that fit much more poorly than the others — most commonly BAYAREALIKE is a much poorer fit, on many datasets)
- "Complex" biogeography: many areas, and thus very large state spaces
- "Complex" setups: many constraints / stratified analyses / strong constraints on areas allowed, dispersal rates, etc.

The usual way the error is observed is that the Maximum Likelihood (ML) search progresses as normal for awhile, trying different values of d, e, and whatever other parameters the user has set to be free. BioGeoBEARS uses either the optim() or optimx() function to conduct this ML search (as specified by the user via the use_optimx option). What these functions are doing is proposing different values of the parameters, calculating the log-likelihood under them, and then iteratively trying other parameter values to see if the log-likelihood improves. This is the classic Maximum Likelihood "heuristic search."

All of this is fine, unless some particular guess at parameter values causes such small probabilities somewhere in the calculation that an underflow error occurs. This could produce a negative probability, an Inf, and/or a NaN (Not a Number) somewhere in the C++ or FORTRAN, which spits an error back to R, which produces a crash.

Usually, in addition to the situations above, the parameter values that are being guessed are "particularly bad" parameter guesses — very small or very large, often near the user-specified limits of the parameters. For both optim() and optimx() in BioGeoBEARS, the "constrained search" option is being used, where each free parameter has limits. These limits are specified by the user in the "min" and "max" columns of the parameters table in the BioGeoBEARS model object. You can see this parameters table with:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table
For reasons that I do not understand — perhaps machine precision, or perhaps something about optim()/optimx()'s attempts to build up the likelihood surface by trying different points — optim() or optimx() may try parameter values just outside of the user-specified limits. As the parameters are usually rates or weights, this could be Very Bad, as negative rates and negative probabilities don't make sense and can cause crashes.

Solution #1: Change the min/max of the parameters

(link to this section)

The solution: The most common, and very successful, solution is to change the min/max bounds on d/e/j (or other parameters) so that they are a little further from 0 or the theoretical max. Usually NaNs occur when the optimx package tries to explore some value that causes some super-small calculated probability that (this is my guess) causes a precision underrun and gets misread as 0 or negative.

Changing the min/max seems to fix the problem because: raising the "min" makes it less likely or impossible that the optim/optimx packages will try values significantly beyond the limit, especially values below 0. Lowering the "max" can have the same effect, in cases where the parameters have theoretical limits.

(Note: in the classic DEC+J format, "j" is a weight that can range between 0 and 3. This means that values above 3 don't make sense, just like values below 0. So, if you change minimum j from, say, 0.00001 to 0.001, I would recommend changing maximum j from 2.99999 to 2.999, just to be self-consistent. However, I suspect that it is the "min" border that is usually the one causing problems.)

(Note also: the limits on "j" should change for DIVALIKE+J (j is between 0 and 2), and BAYAREALIKE+J (j is between 0 and 1). This is because of the numbers of other types of cladogenetic events allowed in these models. See the example script for more details.)

Example code for changing the limits on a parameter:

# Just as you can access the variable type for "j", the initial starting value of "j", etc., like this:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","type"] = "free"

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","init"] = 0.01

# ...you can access the "min" and "max" for "j" (or "d", "e", whatever), like this:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","min"]

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","max"]

# Often, narrowing the limits a teeny bit fixes NaN/Inf problems during the ML search.
#
# You can access the full parameters table with:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table

Solution #2: Use parameter scaling (beta)

(link to this section)

Another possible solution is to use parameter scaling. Here, each free parameter is auto-transformed into a number using a logit transformation (which will change a number on e.g. a 0-1 scale, into a number between -Inf and +Inf; this can be modified to replace 0 and 1 with the user-specified min and max). It is then auto-transformed back into the original parameter space for use in the likelihood calculation.

You can try parameter scaling with:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$rescale_params = TRUE
This should help with the precision underflow issue. However, I have not extensively tested it, so this should be regarded as a beta feature.

Parameter scaling also help with "scaling" warnings sometimes issued by optim() or optimx() when, say, one parameter ranges between 0.001 and 1, and another ranges between 0.001 and 100. The heuristic search methods used by optim() and optimx() are happiest when all parameters have the same scaling.

This might be particularly useful when likelihood surfaces are quite flat for one parameter — I have noticed this sometimes with "+w" models, where dispersal probabilities are being scaled by (manual dispersal multipliers)^w, and sometimes ML with the +w model gets a log-likelihood worse than the log-likelihood found by the default model without w (!!). However, again, I have not tested this extensively.

As always, when running heuristic ML searches, researchers should always be thinking and should always watch out for optimization problems, with BioGeoBEARS or any other program using heuristic ML or Bayesian searches. Some advice on this is found in Issues with Maximum Likelihood (ML) optimization and ML optimization routines and their pitfalls.

=========================

Explanation:

speedup=FALSE runs constrained ML optimization (optimizing parameters within user-specified min/max) on default settings

speedup=TRUE runs constrained ML optimization (optimizing parameters within user-specified min/max) on altered settings (less precision required, fewer iterations checked) that should speed up the search.

Hi XXX -- thanks for the details. Yeah, so I have noticed this on rare occasions, that the ML optimizer is trying values beyond the user-specified limits.  This is some kind of issue with the optim() or optimx() packages, and not something I can fix.

Probably what is happening is that when speedup=FALSE, it is doing the full, more thorough search, and so it tries more values, and eventually (I guess) decides to go outside the bounds for some reason.

The real ML j is almost never at the upper limit, 3, so you could be really bold and just set the max to 2.9 or something. (j=3 would mean every single node is having jump dispersal, which means you have no conservation of ranges on the phylogeny, which means your data are basically random and your biogeographical model probably wouldn't outperform a random-ranges model.)

Regarding DEC+x gets higher LnL than DEC+x+J...

This is *hard proof* of *optimization failure* in that run, because adding a parameter should always improve the likelihood (because DEC+x is just DEC+x+J with j=0).  Link for Google Group readers:

Issues with Maximum Likelihood (ML) optimization
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#optim

This is presumably why you are trying speedup=FALSE etc.

It's possible that optimization failure could be happening because you are getting some kind of interaction between x and j, and this is causing optimization issues. E.g., perhaps x gets more extreme in one direction, and j gets more extreme in another, until the likelihood calculation breaks and the run crashes.  This kind of thing is not uncommon in more complex ML searches, in many different programs. A common term you will see is "likelihood ridge" or "identifiability problems".

Optimization problems could also cause a more extreme search, as the optimizer hunts around for a likelihood peak, since the optimx() and optim() packages are attempting to build up a likelihood surface in order to find the maximum. Perhaps they search right out to the limits of j, and then go a little beyond the limits and crash.

Additional things to try/check, in rough order of likelihood of working:

1. Reset the limits of x so that the max is 0, and the min is -2 or something.  (x > 0 means larger distances have larger dispersal probability, which probably we think we can rule out a priori)

2. Try use_optimx = FALSE (this will switch to optim instead of optimx, sometimes this works better)

3. Start the DEC+x+J search from the optimum values of the DEC+x inference.

4. Especially if you start from #3, and the likelihood goes DOWN, then probably the likelihood surface is too flat for the default algorithm or something.  You can always conduct a manual search:

E.g.,
4a. Start with the ML DEC+x parameters, but leave them free
4b. Copy that model 10 times, but each time pick tight limits on j, e.g.:

j init=0.01, j min=0.099, j max=0.011
j init=0.03, j min=0.029, j max=0.031
j init=0.1, j min=0.099, j max=0.101

...etc...

See which one has the ML, then repeat with a narrower search if you think it is necessary.

5. You could also just do a gridded search, using the skip_optim=TRUE option of bears_optim_run():

bears_optim_run(BioGeoBEARS_run_object, skip_optim=TRUE)

"Gridded search" just means you make a list of possible values of d, e, x, and j, and calculate the likelihood under each combination.  Narrow it down, and repeat as necessary.  It may be that you can cut this down to just x and j, which would help a lot.

Remember: getting the extra few decimal points of the parameter estimate, or the last 0.1 increment of the log-likelihood, isn't all that important.  It's much more important to avoid gross errors (DEC+x+J having lower LnL than DEC+x) than small errors.

6. Scale the distances so that the minimum distance is 1 (i.e., divide by the smallest distance)

7. Don't have any distances of 0 (except diagonals, diagonals are ignored)

8. Think carefully if your distance matrix is *likely* to have decent correlation with dispersal probability, given the number of distances in your distance matrix, and given the amount of data in your tree.  Do sister groups living in different areas tend to be close together geographically, or not?  If yes, there should be signal.  If not, it may be that x=0 is the optimum model.  In Van Dam & Matzke (2016), we actually found that the signal of distance was weak in those clades.  But, there are other datasets where it is very strong.

Cheers!
Nick

As a follow-up to the optimization issues with +x models, a user now has results where DEC+x gives higher LnL than DEC, and DEC+x+J gives higher LnL than DEC+x, but the estimates of "d" and "e" are both 5, for DEC+x and DEC+x+J.  My thoughts on this situation:

====================
You are getting closer -- these look good in terms of the LnLs improving.  HOWEVER -- ...look at "d" and "e" for many of the +x models!  They are spiking up to 5!  That's an average of 5 events per million years, which is ridiculously high unless your tree branches are super-short.

(IIRC your tree was pretty normal, but see the BioGeoBEARS wiki on small trees: http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#fix_short_trees )

The only reason these estimates stopped at "5" is that the default max on d and e is 5.  This means you aren't really at the ML yet, and the true likelihoods will be higher for those models.

I strongly suspect that your distances are interacting with your d and e, as you have a strong negative x. You can imagine, if you had a minimum distance of 1000 km, then if x=-1, all dispersal rates are being multiplied by d_new = d_base * 1000^-1 = dbase / 1000.  This will be a small number, so d might increase by a lot in order to match the number of events on the tree.   If d hits the max limit for d, then the optimizer can't move d all the way to whatever value would maximize the likelihood.

So: I do think that re-scaling the distances, so the minimum distance is 1, will help fix this problem.

An alternative strategy would be to try raising the limits of d and e (it might take a lot! like max=100 or 500 or something).

Cheers, Nick

> > > Probably what is happening is that when speedup=FALSE, it is doing the full, more thorough search, and so it tries more values, and eventually (I guess) decides to go outside the bounds for some reason.

> > >
> > > 3. Start the DEC+x+J search from the optimum values of the DEC+x inference.

> > > 4. Especially if you start from #3, and the likelihood goes DOWN, then probably the likelihood surface is too flat for the default algorithm or something.  You can always conduct a manual search:

> > > E.g.,
> > > 4a. Start with the ML DEC+x parameters, but leave them free
> > > 4b. Copy that model 10 times, but each time pick tight limits on j, e.g.:
> > >
> > > j init=0.01, j min=0.099, j max=0.011
> > > j init=0.03, j min=0.029, j max=0.031
> > > j init=0.1, j min=0.099, j max=0.101
> > >
> > > ...etc...
> > >
> > > See which one has the ML, then repeat with a narrower search if you think it is necessary.
> > >
> > >

messages.body_plain:
Quick answer to a +x question:

On Tue, May 17, 2016 at 6:04 AM, XXX wrote:
> Dear Nick Matzke,
>
> I have a dataset containing fossils and extant taxa as terminals and I would like to run a stratified analysis using different distance matrices for each time bin. I constructed the distance_matrix file (estimating relative distances using paleomaps reconstructions for the chosen periods) and I ran the analysis with and without the J parameter, as in the example script on your wikisites.
>
> However, I was wondering if the distance matrices have any effect without the x-parameter included. I am not very familiar with programming languages and how your software really works, so I was not able to understand if when I load the distance matrices and time periods files the software already consider those distances on the analyses or if it will only consider it when I run an analysis including the x-parameter along with the others.
>
> I thought this was a too dumb question to post on the mailing list, so I decided to send you a personal email asking it.
>
> Thanks in advance.
> Best wishes,
> XXX

---------- Forwarded message ----------
From: Nick Matzke <nickmat...@gmail.com>
Date: Tue, May 17, 2016 at 12:52 PM
Subject: Re: Distance matrices and x-parameter
To: XXX

Hi XXX,

The default of x is 0, so if you load a distance matrix, it will have no effect unless you give x a value different from 0, or make x free.

The +x model works like this:

d_actual = d_base * distance ^ x

If x = 0, this is:

d_actual = d_base * distance ^ 0

d_actual = d_base * 1

d_actual = d_base

(meaning, no effect of distance)

See this paper for the +x model:

Van Dam, Matthew; Matzke, Nicholas J. (2016). Evaluating the influence of connectivity and distance on biogeographic patterns in the south-western deserts of North America. Journal of Biogeography. Special paper, published online 3 March 2016.
http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/jbi.12727 http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/jbi.12727

Cheers!
Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've added several sections to the Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping Example Script wiki page.

KEY THINGS:

1. Run the BSM example script TO THE END and *LOOK* AT THE LAST PAGE OR SO OF SCREEN OUTPUT. (This part is important summary information and counts, all of the stuff before is just keeping track of the progress of stochastic mapping.)

2. Some of the questions I often get were already being answered by the function count_ana_clado_events(), and printed to screen and to the output object "counts_lists".

(I just improved this function a bit today, re-source() http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/summarize_BSM_tables_v1.R to get that.)

3. Phylogenies in APE/R are complex, time-stratification makes it way more complex, and mapping histories on top of all that is even more complex, so it will take some serious personal study/work, and patience and detailed reading, and some personal experimentation (and some R skills), for someone to get a good understanding of the details of the BSM output. Beyond the example script, there is no obvious way to make it easier, as there is a long list of possible things people might want to do.

Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping Example Script
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeographical-stochastic-mapping-example-script

New sections added May 2016:
==============
Interpreting the outputs of Biogeographic Stochastic Mapping
  Accessing all of the summary tables
  Accessing the tables storing all of the actual stochastic maps
  Readings lists and tables in R
The meanings of the column headings of Biogeographic Stochastic Mapping events tables
  The column headings that come from prt() and chainsaw2()
  The meanings of the column headings of clado_events_tables
  The meanings of the column headings of ana_events_tables
==============

The later sections are not a full from-scratch tutorial, but should be helpful to those with enough R skills to query output objects, do for-loops, make their own tables to look at events at specific branches and nodes, etc. (Sometimes people have issues just with understanding how tables and lists work in R, readers in that situation should go do basic R tutorials first.)

Cheers!
Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hi Nick,

could you please tell us briefly what is the difference between your trait dependent dispersal model and the one recently published by Sukumaran et al. <http://sysbio.oxfordjournals.org/content/65/3/525>?

For me it looks like that both approaches test the influence of an trait on dispersal. Your model seems to estimate the parameters during model fitting, whereas the other approach needs to get independently estimated parameters as input. However, neither of them estimates trait dependent speciation rates like in the *SSE models.

Thank you!

Jeet's method is closer to being an Approximate Bayesian Computation-type approach; it relies on forward simulations.  The BioGeoBEARS method is a full likelihood calculation.  This is handy for parameter estimation, standard model choice tools, etc. but will be strongly limited by the size of the state space. Other approaches may be more feasible for larger state spaces.

messages.body_plain:
What do you mean with dispersal event at a node? Dispersal (d of the DEC) are by definition along branches.

If you want to know the frequency of different cladogenetic events (have a look at the supermodel! <http://phylo.wdfiles.com/local--files/biogeobears/BioGeoBEARS_supermodel.png>)  you can perform the following queries on the BSM output:

Node <-  36 # Use Nick's handy prt function to determine your node of interest
Clado <- lapply(BSM_output$RES_clado_events_tables, function(x) x[x$node == Node,])
table(unlist(lapply(Clado, function(x) x$clado_event_type[1])))

If, indeed you want to know about anagenetic dispersal along branches, just subset the anagenetic tables and have a look what is happening upstream of the respective node:

Ana <- lapply(BSM_output$RES_ana_events_tables, function(x) x[x$node == Node,])

HTH

messages.body_plain:
Hi -- thanks for using the group.  "resDEC" stands for "results of DEC".  So you will have to run the DEC model first before running DEC+J, for those lines to work. You must have skipped that section.

That code is there so that the DEC+J search starts at the Maximum Likelihood Estimates (MLE) obtained under the DEC model.  This makes it easy to check if the DEC+J ML solution has a higher log-likelihood than the ML DEC solution.  Adding a parameter should always improve the log-likelihood, but if it doesn't, you have optimization failure (ML searches aren't always perfect).  This bit of code helps the user double-check.

However, if you don't want to run DEC first, just change those lines and pick your own starting values for d and e:

dstart = 0.01
estart = 0.01
jstart = 0.0001

Cheers, Nick
